chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
title: Sandy Williams, and turning down Cab Calloway and Fletcher
summary: He stayed with Hines for the friends and the chance to solo on broadcasts, and refused Calloway, who he felt did not let his men feature.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Sandy and I were very good friends even when I was a Kid kidding around Washington, you know. And he used to always encourage me. In fact, he tried to get me with Fletcher once but I wouldn't go, you know. Because when I was with Earl, it was kind of hard to get me away because I just dug the guys. I dug Budd, and I dug Ray Nance, and Walter Fuller and I were good friends. George Dickson and I -- Wally Bishop --

we all were just real good friends. It wasn't a matter of money because none of them were paying much money. The only bands them that probably was paying more money would be a band like Cab or Duke. You know, those were the only ones in -- I didn't want to work with Cab. He had a lot of good men with him but I always felt -- I could have been wrong -- but I always felt that he didn't give the guys a chance to actually do what they could do.

Even if he wanted to he couldn't because the public was paying for Cab Calloway, and when he didn't do those songs -- "Minny the Moocher" and all those songs, well, they weren't going to support him. If he was going to feature the guys, they didn't know the guys. But we knew how good the guys were. We knew that he had fantastic players with him.

Yeah, but they really didn't -- with Earl's band you had a chance to show yourself, you know, to play. He would let you play. You know, on a broadcast we used to broadcast every night out of the Grand Terrace. And the guys with Cab used to call me all the way from Texas. Say man, that sure is a good trombone player -- solo you played, Trummy. Keg Johnson used to call me -- Budd's brother -- all the time and say, Trummy, that's fantastic. How can you play that high. You know, he used to call me. And these -- this would give you incentive to work on things, you know.

It was real encouragement, you know, for you to do things. And that's why they tried to get me with Cab's band back there then, but I wouldn't go, you know. I told them I wouldn't go. I said if I got with your band, you think I'd get those kind of solos to play. And Cab said, yeah, that makes sense. You'd make money but you wouldn't be -- I didn't need money then. I was foot loose and free, you know, so I didn't need no lot of money and I just enjoyed playing. I really almost didn't go with Lunceford from Earl because I enjoyed the band.
